client: Lately, I’ve been feeling completely overwhelmed trying to balance my graduate program and my part-time job at the coffee shop. I want to excel in my studies, but I’m constantly worried that I’m not doing enough, and then I feel guilty when I’m at work because I’m distracted by school. Honestly, I’m not sure if therapy can really help with this—it feels like there’s just too much to handle and no easy way out.
therapist: It sounds like you’re carrying a lot of weight right now, feeling pulled in different directions and unsure how to manage it all. When you say you’re worried about not doing enough, what kind of thoughts come up for you about what “enough” looks like?

client: I keep comparing myself to my classmates who seem to be reading every paper and participating in every seminar while I'm just scraping by. "Enough" would be staying on campus until midnight like some of them do, but honestly that thought just makes me feel exhausted. And then when I'm at work, I beat myself up for not using that time to study instead.
therapist: It sounds like you’re holding yourself to a really high standard, and the comparison to others is adding to that pressure. I wonder if we could explore what feels realistic for you, rather than what others are doing—what would “enough” look like if it were based on your own needs and energy?

client: That’s hard to answer because I don’t even know what my own needs are anymore. I feel like I’ve been on autopilot for so long, just trying to get through each day. If I try to set my own standard, I worry I’ll end up being lazy or falling behind—it feels safer to push myself harder, even if it’s unsustainable.
therapist: It sounds like you’re stuck in a cycle where pushing yourself feels safer, even though it’s leaving you drained and disconnected from your own needs. Let’s pause for a moment—what would it feel like to imagine “enough” as something that supports your well-being, rather than something that keeps you running on autopilot?

client: Honestly, the idea of focusing on my well-being instead of productivity makes me anxious—like I'm setting myself up to fail. But at the same time, I'm so tired of this constant pressure. Maybe if "enough" meant getting adequate sleep while still submitting decent work, that might feel... slightly less impossible? But I don't trust myself not to take it too far and slack off.
therapist: It sounds like you’re caught between wanting to ease the pressure and fearing what might happen if you let go of it even a little. That tension can feel paralyzing. What would it look like to take one small step toward balance—like prioritizing sleep—without labeling it as “slacking off”? How could we reframe that as taking care of yourself to perform better in the long run?

client: I guess I could try getting more sleep, but it feels like I’m giving up something important—like I’ll lose my edge or fall behind. And part of me thinks, “What if I sleep more and still don’t do well? Then I’ll have wasted time.” It’s hard to see self-care as productive when I’ve always equated success with sacrificing everything else.
therapist: It sounds like there’s a deep fear tied to letting go of that edge, even though it’s costing you so much. The idea of self-care feels risky because it challenges a belief you’ve held for a long time—that success requires sacrifice. What do you think it would take to start seeing self-care not as giving up, but as a way to build resilience for the challenges ahead?

client: I don't know if I can ever really believe self-care helps with success when all the messages I've gotten—from professors, my family, even myself—say otherwise. Maybe if I saw actual proof that taking breaks helped instead of hurt my performance... but that would mean taking a risk I'm scared to take. It's like my whole identity is wrapped up in being the person who pushes through exhaustion.
therapist: It sounds like this fear of letting go is deeply rooted, and the messages you’ve internalized make it feel even harder to trust that self-care could be valuable. What if we approached this as an experiment—testing whether small changes, like taking short breaks or prioritizing sleep, could actually enhance your performance without risking your identity as someone who works hard? How would it feel to try that, just to see what happens?

client: An experiment sounds less scary than fully committing to change, I guess. But even small breaks make me feel guilty—like I'm wasting time I could be working. What if I try it and it backfires? Then I'll have proof that pushing myself was the right way all along. That thought terrifies me more than continuing like this.
therapist: It sounds like the fear of being wrong about this is almost as overwhelming as the pressure itself—like experimenting with breaks could confirm your worst fears about needing to push yourself. That’s a heavy weight to carry. What would it feel like to approach this experiment with curiosity rather than certainty, letting yourself explore without needing it to prove anything definitive right away?

client: Curiosity sounds nice in theory, but it feels like a luxury I can’t afford right now. I’m so used to judging everything I do—either it’s productive or it’s wasted time. Letting go of that judgment feels almost impossible, like I’d be losing control over my progress. I don’t know if I can trust myself to explore without spiraling into guilt.
therapist: It sounds like the fear of losing control is holding you back, and the idea of letting go of judgment feels overwhelming right now. That’s okay—this is a big shift, and it’s natural to feel cautious. What if we started small, like taking just one intentional break this week and noticing how it feels afterward? Could we explore that together without labeling it as “good” or “bad”?

client: I could try one break, I guess... but I already know I'll spend the whole time thinking about what I *should* be doing instead. Even now, I'm mentally calculating how many minutes this conversation is taking away from my reading. It's exhausting to feel this way, but stopping feels just as scary. Maybe if I scheduled a specific short break? Though that makes it feel like another task to fail at.
therapist: It sounds like even the idea of taking a break brings up a lot of tension for you, as if it’s just another thing to manage or fail at. That’s a heavy burden to carry—always feeling like you’re running out of time or not doing enough. What would it feel like to approach this first break not as a task, but as a moment to pause and breathe, even if it’s just for a few minutes? Could we explore what that might look like for you?

client: A pause to breathe sounds... impossible right now. Even the idea makes my chest tighten because I know the work will still be waiting afterward. But I'm also so tired of feeling like this—maybe if I tried it during my commute home? Though I'll probably just spend that time mentally listing everything I didn't finish today.
therapist: It sounds like even the thought of pausing brings up a lot of tension and worry about what’s left undone—like you’re carrying the weight of unfinished tasks with you everywhere. That must feel exhausting. What if we reframe this pause not as a way to avoid work, but as a moment to recharge so you can approach what’s next with a clearer mind? How would it feel to experiment with that idea during your commute, even if it’s just noticing one thing around you?
